Tensor Analysis – Practical 5 Solutions Information: • Please make sure to complete all exercises before the next lecture. • The exercises marked with [See lecture] were solved in class. • The exercises are not organised by difficulty. 5.1 [See Lecture] Write down the transformation rule for: (1) a tensor of rank four, (2) a tensor of rank six. Solution: Rank four: Tijkℓ = LiaLjbLkcLℓdTabcd. Rank six: Rijkℓmn = LiaLjbLkcLℓdLmeLnf Rabcdef . 5.2 If Qijkℓ is a tensor of rank four, show that Qijjℓ is a tensor of rank two. Solution: As Qijkℓ is a tensor of rank four, it satisfies Q ′ ijkℓ = LimLjnLkpLℓqQmnpq. Hence Q ′ ijjℓ = LimLjnLjpLℓqQmnpq = LimδnpLℓqQmnpq ( using LjnLjp = δnp) = LimLℓqQmnnq, which gives the result. 1

# Page 2^page=2
2 5.3 [See lecture] If Tij is a tensor, show that Tii is a scalar. Solution: Since Tij is a tensor, we know that T ′ ij = LikLjmTkm. Therefore T ′ ii = LikLimTkm = δkmTkm = Tmm = Tii, where the last equality comes from the fact that we can replace a dummy index with another dummy index. 5.4 Consider the 2D polar coordinates (x1, x2) = (r, θ). In this system, the position vector r is given by r = r cos θ i1 + r sin θ i2, where i1, i2 are the usual 2-dimensional Cartesian basis vectors. (1) Find the corresponding basis vectors e1 and e2. (2) Find the covariant metric tensor gij and give your answer as a 2 × 2 matrix. Using the fact that the basis e1, e2 is orthogonal, find the contravariant metric tensor gij. (3) Give an expression for the arc length of the polar coordinate system, plus explicitly state the metric coefficients h1, h2. Solution: (1) Remember that ei = ∂r ∂xi . Thus, e1 = ∂r ∂x1 = ∂r ∂r = cos θ i1 + sin θ i2, e2 = ∂r ∂x2 = ∂r ∂θ = −r sin θ i1 + r cos θ i2. (2) Using the result in (1), we obtain g11 = e1 · e1 = cos 2 θ + sin2 θ = 1, g22 = e2 · e2 = r2 sin 2 θ + r2 sin 2 θ = r2, g12 = e1 · e2 = g21 = e2 · e1 = 0. In matrix form gij = ( 1 0 0 r2 ) .

# Page 3^page=3
3 Using orthogonality, we have gii = 1/gii for each i = 1, 2. Thus gij = ( 1 0 0 1/r2 ) (3) The element of the arc length is (ds) 2 = gijdxidxj = g11dx1dx1 + g22dx2dx2 = (dr) 2 + (rdθ)2. Hence the metric coefficients are h1 = 1, h2 = r. 5.5 In spherical coordinates (x1, x2, x3) = (r, ϕ, θ), the position vector r is given by r = r sin ϕ cos θ i1 + r sin ϕ sin θ i2 + r cos ϕ i3. Find the basis vectors and the metric coefficients. Solution: We have e1 = ∂r ∂r = sin ϕ cos θ i1 + sin ϕ sin θ i2 + cos ϕ i3 e2 = ∂r ∂ϕ = r cos ϕ cos θ i1 + r cos ϕ sin θ i2 − r sin ϕ i3 e3 = ∂r ∂θ = −r sin ϕ sin θi1 + r sin ϕ cos θ i2. Hence the element of the arc length is (ds)2 = (dr) 2 + (rdϕ) 2 + (r sin ϕ dθ) 2 The metric coefficients are then h1 = 1, h2 = r, h3 = r sin ϕ.

# Page 4^page=4
4 5.6 [See Lecture] Given two vectors A and B, with components Ai and Bi, show that the second-order tensor with components Cik = AiBk − AkBi is antisymmetric. Solution: We must show Cik = −Cki. We have Cki = AkBi − AiBk = −(AiBk − AkBi) = −Cik. 5.7 [Question from the Main Exam 23-24] The third-rank tensor Tijk is symmetric with respect to its last two suffixes but antisymmetric with respect to its first and second suffices. Show that all entries of this tensor are zero (i.e. Tijk = 0, for all choices of i,j,k). Solution: One the one hand, Tijk = −Tjik = −Tjki. On the other hand, Tijk = Tikj = −Tkij = −Tkji = −(−Tjki) = Tjki. Consequently, −Tjki = Tjki, and therefore Tjki = 0, as required. 5.8 Let q1, q2, q3 be coordinates related to orthogonal coordinates x1, x2, x3 with orthonormal basis i1, i2, i3 by the formulae q1 = x1 + x2, q2 = x1 − x2, q3 = 2x3. (1) Find the corresponding basis vectors and show that they form an orthogonal basis. [Hint: Using r = x1i1 + x2i2 + x3i3, you need to find expressions for x1, x2, x3 in terms of q1, q2, q3 and substitute these into your expansion for r.] (2) Find the metric tensor gik and give your answer as a matrix. Using the fact that the basis e1, e2, e3 is orthogonal, find the contravariant metric tensor gik. (3) Give an expression for the arc length of the coordinate system with respect to the basis e1, e2, e3. (4) Find the covariant and contravariant components of the vectors A = 2i1, B = i1 + i2, C = 2i1 − 3i3, with respect to the basis e1, e2, e3, but without computing the dual basis e1, e2, e3.

# Page 5^page=5
5 Solution: (1) We have the position vector r = x1i1 + x2i2 + x3i3 is given by r = q1 + q2 2 i1 + q1 − q2 2 i2 + q3 2 i3. Hence the basis vectors are given by e1 = ∂r ∂q1 = i1 2 + i2 2 , e2 = ∂r ∂q2 = i1 2 − i2 2 , e3 = ∂r ∂q3 = i3 2 . Clearly one has ei · ek = 0 when i ̸= k, hence the basis is orthogonal. (2) The metric tensor gik is given by [gik] =   1/2 0 0 0 1/2 0 0 0 1/4   . Now as we are dealing with an orthogonal basis, we have gii = 1/gii. Thus [gik] =   2 0 0 0 2 0 0 0 4   . (3) As the basis e1, e2, e3 is orthogonal the formula for the arc length is (ds) 2 = g11dq1dq1 + g22dq2dq2 + g33dq3dq3, hence (ds)2 = 1 2 dq1dq1 + 1 2 dq2dq2 + 1 4 dq3dq3. (4) Consider A = 2i1. As Ai = A · ei, we have A1 = 1, A2 = 1, A3 = 0. Then using the relation Ai = giiAi (no summation), we obtain A 1 = g11A1 = 2 A 2 = g22A2 = 2 A 3 = g33A3 = 0.

6 Similarly one has B1 = 1, B2 = 0, B3 = 0, B1 = 2, B2 = 0, B3 = 0 and C1 = 1, C2 = 1, C3 = −3/2, C1 = 2, C2 = 2, C3 = −6. 5.9 Given two generalised coordinate systems, with bases e1, e2, e3 and e′ 1, e′ 2, e′ 3, respec- tively, suppose that the position vector x has coordinates (x1, x2, x3) with respect to e1, e2, e3 and suppose that x has coordinates (x′1, x′2, x′3) with respect to e′ 1, e′ 2, e′ 3. Let L j i′ be the coefficients of the direct transformation and L j′ i the coefficients of the inverse transformation. Given the following alternative definitions: L j i′ = ∂xj ∂x′i , L i′ j = ∂x′i ∂xj , show that g.j i = L k′ i L j k′. Solution: We have Lk′ i L j k′ = ∂x′k ∂xi ∂xj ∂x′k = ∂xj ∂xi = δ.j i , as required (using the notation for generalised coordinate systems).
